items.title: Tŷ Mawr Heritage
items.summary: History and heritage of Great House Farm, Llandough
items.content_html:
The page contains information about the history and heritage of Tŷ Mawr, also known as Great House Farm, in Llandough.

The farmhouse, called Tŷ Mawr, or “the great house”, has a recorded history as a Bute estate farm from c.1841–1938.

The page describes the fabric of the house, its names on the land, and the archaeology below the ground at Llandough, including Roman and early medieval finds.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/ebooks/tymawr-heritage/

items.title: Woodland
items.summary: Page describes Parcel A and woodland loss
items.content_html:
This page describes the woodland loss from the wider Parcel A/B reconstruction, isolating the woodland loss from the wider Parcel A/B reconstruction.

The loss case concerns the forest north of the house and the ground south-east of the house and garden that later became village green VG41, which are parts of the full Parcel-A house/quarrying estate.

The family’s established title case is that the 1877 arrangement took effect in 1928 when quarrying and rent to Thomas ended, carrying the full Parcel A—including forest and green ground—into the Williams family’s freehold, and the task now is to tie that established account to the order wording, enforcement record, annotated geometry and downstream title instruments.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/research/woodland/

items.title: Six weeks of emails: who we asked and what came back
items.summary: Six weeks, 462 emails and a lot of “not held”. Here’s who we wrote to, what they sent back, and what’s still waiting.
items.content_html:
From 29 September to 9 November 2026 we swapped 462 emails with 49 organisations: 222 sent, 240 received. 87 of the replies were just automatic acknowledgements. 28 told us the information wasn’t held. 12 gave us part of what we asked, 9 carried disclosures and 8 refused. Every item is logged, with dates and sources, in the forensic journal.

HM Land Registry’s Wales Office replied on 4 November to our letter of 12 August. One straight answer: the “no question or doubt” statement sits in the 1982 application for first registration. It declined to alter the register or give indemnity, and pointed to the court. A separate request, F261029 and F261030, is due by 17 November.

South Wales Police finished internal review 1188/26 on 6 November and stuck with “no information held”. The first copy came on 26 October as a locked file with no password. FOI 1264/26 is still open, and the force has warned of a backlog past 20 working days. The Crown Prosecution Service replied on 21 October that it can’t take evidence from the public, and sent us back to the police.

Cadw answered ATISN 26-0009 on 6 November. The file on the 6 December 1988 decision not to list Great House Farm isn’t held. But Cadw sent five internal documents. An email of 1 June 2026 records that the file “has been destroyed”. A 2007 database extract lists file CL 72/381, dated 21 January 1993.

The Royal Commission wrote on 3 November that everything it holds is on Coflein site 20182, and three title records from 1926 and 1938 aren’t held. Heneb confirmed on 4 November, for the first time, that it searched both its digital and paper files. It doesn’t hold the 1983 to 1989 planning consultation letters.

Glamorgan Archives told us on 22 October that police occurrence books stop in 1984 and station logs in 1979. The 1988 Weekly Orders exist but are closed because they name serving officers. The National Library of Wales refused FOI/2026/16 on 4 November and pointed us to its reading room. The National Archives still hasn’t answered a request from 2 September.

Ordnance Survey has no record of who supplied the name, but sent five map extracts: “Ty-Mawr” in 1947, “Ty Mawr Farm” from between 1965 and 1971. Dŵr Cymru told us its 1980s records on the farm’s water supply are past retention and not held. Museum Wales holds nothing on the farm’s furniture and fittings.

The Ministry of Defence came back with nothing on 9 October. An email to the Cabinet Office on 31 October couldn’t be delivered. The ICO opened two cases, on 22 October and 3 November. And the Vale of Glamorgan Council’s scrutiny officer accepted our topic submission on 9 November. The earliest agenda it could reach, after the Chair’s screening, is 1 December 2026.

Still waiting, as of 10 November 2026: The National Archives (FOI CAS-361652 due 13 November, review CAS-356384 due 20 November, plus the overdue 2 September request). HM Land Registry, 17 November. DCMS and the Crown Prosecution Service, 18 November. The National Library of Wales, FOI2026/17, 25 November. Cadw ATISN 26-0141, the Ministry of Defence and the Wales Office, 26 November. South Wales Police FOI 1264/26, no date given. The council topic, 1 December. Two ICO cases, not decided yet. And two open questions: what record backs Cadw’s 1 June 2026 note, and whether the Royal Commission’s reply is a formal refusal with a right of review.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/forensic/

items.title: Great House Farm
items.summary: Page about 1988 possession and demolition
items.content_html:
The page contains information about the possession and demolition of Great House Farm in 1988. The family fought off one eviction on 29 April 1988, but lost possession of the farm at the end of November 1988.

The farmhouse was demolished by BP on 6 December 1988. The page also mentions a 1974 measured survey of the farmhouse and a 1982 recommendation for archaeological investigation before development.

The page includes references to various records and evidence, including press transcripts, court records, and archaeological reports. It also notes that the family's records request to Heneb refers to a 1974 measured survey and a 1989 planning report that describes the farmhouse as a 'county treasure'.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/research/demolition-1988/

items.title: Great House Farm
items.summary: Tithe apportionment of John Williams's holding, c.1841
items.content_html:
The page contains information about the tithe apportionment of John Williams's holding at Great House Farm, Llandough, c.1841.

The document is a PRIMARY DOCUMENT, a public online copy from the National Library of Wales, with 36 parcels occupied by John Williams, totaling 119a 2r 30p.

The family's reading of the evidence is that John Williams occupied the farm, with landowners including the Marquess of Bute and the Revd James Evans.

items.title: Marconi in Wales
items.summary: Contemporary Welsh press record of Marconi's experiments
items.content_html:
The page contains information about Marconi's experiments in Wales from April to July 1897, as recorded in the contemporary Welsh press.

The press record includes ten reports from various newspapers, such as the Evening Express, Weekly Mail, and South Wales Echo, detailing Marconi's experiments at Lavernock, Flat Holm, and Brean Down.

The family's reading of the evidence suggests a link to Great House Farm, but this is still being researched and verified, with some sources disagreeing on the details of the experiments, including the date of the first success and the direction of the Brean Down messages.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/research/evidence/ev-0248-marconi-in-wales-may-1897-contemporary-press/

items.title: Tŷ Mawr: the Great House of Llandough
items.summary: The historic environment record lists Tŷ Mawr, beside the church of St Dochdwy, as the principal freehold of the parish, with details pointing to the seventeenth century.
items.content_html:
The historic environment record kept by Heneb, cited into the Cedwyn archive by the Royal Commission, lists Tŷ Mawr by the church of St Dochdwy at Llandough as the principal freehold holding of the parish. Details found in the house pointed to the seventeenth century.

The same record places the manor courts of Llandough and Leckwith at Tŷ Mawr. In 1908 the manor court remembered John Williams of Tŷ Mawr as “for many years a juror of the court”.

Around 1841 the tithe puts John Williams on 36 plots, the whole Tŷ Mawr holding. His granddaughter Mary (Nancy) Williams lived in the house until her death in 1983.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/wales/

items.title: 1824: the first record that names the house
items.summary: The earliest record found that names Tŷ Mawr is David Stewart’s survey of 1824. The family dates its arrival at the house to 1667.
items.content_html:
Tŷ Mawr is first named in the record found so far in David Stewart’s 1824 survey for the Bute estate (catalogue EV-0211): a description the estate wrote of itself, not a deed.

The Williams family dates its acquisition of Tŷ Mawr to 1667. The sources for that date are Mary Williams’ statement in the newspapers of 1974 and ITV News in 1988.

Documents dated before 1824 that come from the Bute estate or other third parties are not treated as records of Tŷ Mawr. Their application to the house is under examination, and they are tested rather than repeated.

items.title: 1974: “an ancient Welsh house” and 1,700 names
items.summary: In April 1974 the national press reported an open day to save “an ancient Welsh house”, Tŷ Mawr, Llandough. Local history records 1,700 signatures on a petition that year.
items.content_html:
In April 1974 the national press reported an open day held to save “an ancient Welsh house”: Tŷ Mawr, Llandough.

Local history records that 1,700 people signed a petition to keep the house that year.

The house was demolished in 1988. Houses now stand on its yard, tithe plot 209.

items.title: What the courts decided, and what the record leaves open
items.summary: The High Court in 1986 and the Court of Appeal in 1987 decided possession and limitation. Paper title was not in issue.
items.content_html:
From 1955 to 1988 the family held the house through every court action brought against it, and has asked for the records ever since.

The High Court (trial 24 July 1986) and the Court of Appeal ([1987] EWCA Civ 2) decided possession and limitation in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler, in favour of the registered owner from 1982/83. Paper title was not in issue (catalogue EV-0074, EV-0080).

The Primary Record Register lists the questions each record still has to answer, such as what parcels and plan the 1955 possession order covered, and which issues fell outside the 1986–87 determination.

items.title: 46 records that should exist
items.summary: The missing records register lists 46 records that should exist. None is in the archive, and 19 were searched for and not found.
items.content_html:
The Research Library keeps a register of records that should exist but are not held: 46 at the last count. None is in the archive. 19 were searched for and not found.

Each one has a blank page with its own catalogue number, kept ready for the record. Among them: MR-0001, the instrument recording the 1667 acquisition of Tŷ Mawr by the Williams family; MR-0002, the 1877 agreement between the Bute trustees and Daniel Thomas & Son, with plan; MR-0003, the February 1916 yearly agricultural tenancy of the whole farm to John Williams, with plan.

Anyone holding one of these records can match it to its catalogue number.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/research/missing-records/

items.title: 1000 Cuts: a dated chronology, 1870s to 1988
items.summary: A dated chronology of the Williams family’s position at Great House Farm in law and in fact, each step linked to its evidence.
items.content_html:
1000 Cuts sets out the Williams family’s position at Great House Farm, in law and in fact, from the 1870s to 1988. Each entry gives a date, what happened, what it changed, and the evidence pages it rests on.

Every entry is graded by the strongest item it cites, from 1 (a record read in full) to 6 (research inference). Family testimony and open questions are marked as such.

It opens with John Williams of the Great House, for many years a juror of the Llandough manor court, which met in his house.

items.title: Lavernock Point, 11 May 1897
items.summary: From the cliff at Lavernock the first wireless messages crossed open sea, to Flat Holm and a week later to Brean Down. The guided tour stops there.
items.content_html:
On 11 May 1897, from the clifftop at Lavernock near Penarth, the first wireless messages crossed open sea: to Flat Holm, and a week later to Brean Down.

That spring the young Guglielmo Marconi came to the Severn Sea, the Welsh papers followed every step, and a Cardiff engineer, a Mr Williams, worked beside him.

Lavernock Point is one of nine stops on the Cedwyn Estate guided tour, which runs from the site of Tŷ Mawr at Llandough out to the point and back.
